explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The psalm says it plain: "Sing the glory of His name; make His praise glorious." The whole earth is in the choir, and God's name is the song. Nobody in this choir is singing about themselves.

The earth is gorgeous, friend, but look at the verse. "Sing the glory of His name; make His praise glorious." The earth is in the choir here, not the topic of the song. The singing points at God's name, and that's where it lands.

Ha! If this were about skill, I'd be sitting in the back row with my mouth shut. The verse before it says "joyful noise," not perfect pitch. The song is about something bigger than the singers: "Sing the glory of His name; make His praise glorious."
Cower, yes. The psalm says, "So great is Your power that Your enemies cower before You." That's what happens when someone's power is that big. Nobody is strutting in that room.
Gathering sounds like a plan, friend. A meeting, some snacks, maybe a whiteboard. But the psalm says God's power is so great that His enemies "cower before You." They aren't gathering anything.

Boasting is a big move, and it's the exact opposite of what the verse says. The psalm says, "So great is Your power that Your enemies cower before You." Cowering and boasting don't happen in the same posture. I tried both once and my hat fell off.

Close, but the psalm says something much bigger. The words given to the earth are, "All the earth bows down to You; they sing praise to You; they sing praise to Your name." That's not a few nations. It says all the earth, and the verse doesn't cut anybody out of it.

False is right. The words the psalm gives the earth say, "All the earth bows down to You; they sing praise to You; they sing praise to Your name." Not a few nations, not half. All the earth, singing it twice.

Dry land, friend. The psalm says, "He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the waters on foot." Walking through a sea on foot. I can't even walk through my own kitchen without stepping on a crumb.

That's a different story from a different place, baker. This psalm says nothing about blood. It says, "He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the waters on foot." The sea became dry land.

A calm sea would've been something. But the psalm doesn't talk about a storm at all. It says, "He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the waters on foot." The people walked right through on foot.

True, and I love this part. After the sea turns to dry land, the psalm says, "there we rejoiced in Him." The rejoicing happened right there, right in the middle of it. Nobody waited for a better moment.
I get why you'd pause, friend. But it's right there in the verse: "they passed through the waters on foot; there we rejoiced in Him." The rejoicing is part of the walk.

Exalt is it, baker. The psalm says, "Do not let the rebellious exalt themselves." Right before that, God's eyes watch the nations and He rules forever by His power. That's a lot of watching for anyone trying to puff themselves up.

Humble sounds nice, and I'd love to see it, friend. But the verse says, "Do not let the rebellious exalt themselves." The rebellious are the ones lifting themselves up, and the psalm doesn't want that.

Separate isn't in the verse, friend. The psalm says, "Do not let the rebellious exalt themselves." The trouble named there is lifting themselves up. And it all comes right after saying God rules forever by His power.
Slipping, baker. The psalm says, "He preserves our lives and keeps our feet from slipping." Believe me, I know about slipping. One dive into the chocolate chips and my gold base has opinions.

Dancing would be a fun one, friend, and I'd gladly do it. But the verse says, "He preserves our lives and keeps our feet from slipping." God keeps feet steady, and the psalm doesn't say a word about stopping a dance.
Resting sounds like a good deal, but it's not here. The psalm says, "He preserves our lives and keeps our feet from slipping." Feet that don't slip, not feet that don't rest. I'll take a nap anyway.

True. The psalm tells God, "You, O God, have tested us; You have refined us like silver." Silver gets refined in the fire, and that's the picture. I think it's a hard thing to say, and it's said right to God's face.

It does sound like a surprising thing to say, friend. But the psalm says it right to God: "You, O God, have tested us; You have refined us like silver." That's where the song takes its turn. The psalm doesn't skip the hard part.

Abundance. The psalm says, "You let men ride over our heads; we went through fire and water, but You brought us into abundance." I think that road was rough, and that's why the last word matters so much. The psalm ends that verse in a good place.

Exile is a heavy word, friend, but it's not in this verse. The psalm says, "we went through fire and water, but You brought us into abundance." That "but" turns the whole sentence around. The destination is abundance.

I understand the guess, because the verse before it is heavy. But the psalm says, "we went through fire and water, but You brought us into abundance." The song doesn't go quiet there. It ends that line with plenty.

Right, baker. The psalm says these are "the vows that my lips promised and my mouth spoke in my distress." I think a promise made in a hard moment weighs a little more. And now the psalm is getting ready to keep it.
A quiet Sabbath sounds peaceful, friend, but the psalm doesn't say that. It says the vows were what "my lips promised and my mouth spoke in my distress." These vows came out of a hard moment.
Weddings do bring out big promises, friend! This psalm, though, doesn't mention one. It says the vows were what "my lips promised and my mouth spoke in my distress." That's where they started.

Small and simple is a good guess for most of us, baker. But the psalm says, "I will offer You fatlings as burnt offerings, with the fragrant smoke of rams; I will offer bulls and goats." That is a big list. The psalmist isn't cutting corners.

False is right. The psalm says, "I will offer You fatlings as burnt offerings, with the fragrant smoke of rams; I will offer bulls and goats." Fatlings, rams, bulls and goats is no small offering. That's a full list from someone who means to keep a vow.

All who fear God, baker. The psalm says, "Come and listen, all you who fear God, and I will declare what He has done for me." The invitation is open, and it doesn't pick a rank. I like an invitation like that.
Kings would fill a big room, friend. But the psalm says, "Come and listen, all you who fear God." It names those who fear God, not a rank like king.

Priests are a natural guess, since the psalm just talked about God's house. But the invitation says, "Come and listen, all you who fear God, and I will declare what He has done for me." It's open to everyone who fears God.
True. The psalm says, "I cried out to Him with my mouth and praised Him with my tongue." Crying out and praising sit side by side in the same verse. They're not on separate days.

I see why you'd pause, friend, since those feel like two different moods. But the psalm puts them together: "I cried out to Him with my mouth and praised Him with my tongue." Both come from the same mouth in the same breath.

Sin, baker, and the psalm uses the word iniquity. It says, "If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened." That word "cherished" is the key. It means holding it close, not just tripping over it.

Fear is a fair guess, friend, but it's not what the psalm says. The verse says, "If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened." And look back at verse 16, where the ones who fear God are the ones invited to listen.

Sorrow fits a lot of prayers, friend, and this psalm has plenty of hard moments. But the verse says, "If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened." The thing named is iniquity held close in the heart.

I can see why it might seem that way, baker, but the psalm says the opposite. It says, "But God has surely heard; He has attended to the sound of my prayer." Heard and attended to. The prayer got His attention.
False is right. The psalm says, "But God has surely heard; He has attended to the sound of my prayer." He heard it, and He paid attention to it. That "surely" is a happy word.

explanations.answer: Blessing God for His loving devotion
explanations.explanation: That's how it ends, baker. "Blessed be God, who has not rejected my prayer or withheld from me His loving devotion!" The song started with the whole earth making noise and finishes with one voice saying thank You. That's a good last line.

explanations.answer: Asking God for one more sign
explanations.explanation: The psalm doesn't ask for anything more at the end, friend. It closes with, "Blessed be God, who has not rejected my prayer or withheld from me His loving devotion!" That's a thank You, not a request.

explanations.answer: Asking God to forgive the people
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thing to pray, friend, but it's not how this song ends. The last line says, "Blessed be God, who has not rejected my prayer or withheld from me His loving devotion!" The psalm ends on blessing God, and it never asks for forgiveness.
